markers.title: Weimar Golden Age
markers.description: A period of relative stability and cultural flourishing in Germany. Jewish businesses and cultural institutions thrive in Berlin.
markers.longDescription: Following the hyperinflation crisis of 1923, Germany entered a period of relative economic stability and cultural renaissance known as the Golden Twenties. Berlin became a center of modernist art, literature, and music. Jewish entrepreneurs, artists, and intellectuals played significant roles in this cultural flowering, with many establishing successful businesses and cultural institutions throughout the city.

markers.title: The Great Depression
markers.description: The Wall Street Crash triggers a global economic crisis. Mass unemployment creates fertile ground for extremist politics in Germany.
markers.longDescription: The stock market crash of October 1929 plunged the world into economic depression. Germany, heavily dependent on American loans, was hit particularly hard. By 1932, unemployment reached 6 million. The economic crisis destabilized the Weimar Republic and created conditions for the rise of extremist political movements, including the Nazi Party.

markers.title: Hitler Appointed Chancellor
markers.description: Adolf Hitler is appointed Chancellor of Germany, marking the beginning of Nazi rule and systematic persecution of Jews.
markers.longDescription: On January 30, 1933, President Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler as Chancellor of Germany. Within weeks, the Nazis began consolidating power, suspending civil liberties, and implementing anti-Jewish policies. This date marks the beginning of state-sponsored persecution that would ultimately devastate Berlin's Jewish community and their businesses.

markers.title: Nazi Boycott of Jewish Businesses
markers.description: The Nazi regime organizes a nationwide boycott of Jewish-owned businesses, marking the first large-scale anti-Jewish action.
markers.longDescription: On April 1, 1933, the Nazi regime organized a nationwide boycott of Jewish-owned shops, department stores, offices, and other businesses. SA storm troopers stood menacingly outside Jewish establishments, discouraging customers from entering. Though the boycott officially lasted only one day, it set a precedent for increasingly severe economic persecution and signaled to German Jews that their livelihoods were no longer secure.

markers.title: Nuremberg Laws
markers.description: The Nuremberg Laws strip German Jews of citizenship and prohibit marriages between Jews and non-Jews.
markers.longDescription: The Nuremberg Laws, announced at the Nazi Party rally in September 1935, institutionalized racial discrimination. The Reich Citizenship Law stripped Jews of German citizenship, while the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honor prohibited marriages and sexual relations between Jews and non-Jews. These laws created a legal framework for further persecution and economic exclusion of Jewish citizens.

markers.title: Aryanization Decree
markers.description: Jews are required to register all property over 5,000 Reichsmarks, facilitating forced sales and seizure of businesses.
markers.longDescription: The Decree on the Registration of Jewish Property required all Jews to register assets exceeding 5,000 Reichsmarks. This law paved the way for systematic 'Aryanization' - the forced transfer of Jewish-owned businesses to non-Jewish Germans at drastically reduced prices. Many Jewish business owners were compelled to sell their life's work for a fraction of its value.

markers.title: Kristallnacht
markers.description: The Night of Broken Glass - a coordinated pogrom destroying thousands of Jewish businesses, synagogues, and homes.
markers.longDescription: On the night of November 9-10, 1938, Nazi paramilitaries and civilians carried out a coordinated pogrom against Jews throughout Germany and Austria. Over 7,500 Jewish-owned businesses were destroyed, synagogues were burned, and approximately 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps. This marked a dramatic escalation in anti-Jewish violence and effectively ended Jewish business ownership in Germany.

markers.title: Jews Banned from Business
markers.description: All remaining Jewish businesses are ordered closed. Jews are prohibited from operating retail stores, workshops, or market stalls.
markers.longDescription: Just days after Kristallnacht, the Decree on the Exclusion of Jews from German Economic Life prohibited Jews from operating any retail, mail-order, or independent craft businesses as of January 1, 1939. Jews were also banned from selling goods or services at markets of any kind. This decree marked the final elimination of Jewish economic participation in German society.

markers.title: World War II Begins
markers.description: Germany invades Poland, beginning World War II. Conditions for remaining Jews in Germany become increasingly dire.
markers.longDescription: Germany's invasion of Poland on September 1, 1939 marked the beginning of World War II in Europe. For Jews remaining in Germany, the war brought new restrictions, including curfews, confiscation of radios and vehicles, and reduced food rations. The outbreak of war also made emigration nearly impossible, trapping many who had hoped to escape.

markers.title: Deportations from Berlin Begin
markers.description: Mass deportations of Berlin Jews to ghettos and concentration camps in the East begin.
markers.longDescription: In October 1941, the Nazi regime began systematic deportations of Jews from Berlin to ghettos and concentration camps in Eastern Europe. The first transports went to the Lodz ghetto. By the war's end, over 55,000 Berlin Jews had been deported, with the vast majority murdered in the Holocaust. The vibrant Jewish community that had built the businesses documented here was nearly completely destroyed.

markers.title: End of World War II in Europe
markers.description: Germany surrenders unconditionally. Of Berlin's pre-war Jewish population of 160,000, only about 8,000 survived.
markers.longDescription: Germany's unconditional surrender on May 8, 1945 ended World War II in Europe. The liberation revealed the full extent of the Holocaust's devastation. Of Berlin's pre-war Jewish population of approximately 160,000, only about 8,000 had survived - most in hiding or through mixed marriages. The businesses, institutions, and community documented in this project had been almost entirely destroyed.
